summary: Yahweh tells Moses that one more plague will cause Pharaoh to drive Israel out and instructs the people to ask Egyptian neighbors for silver and gold. Moses announces that firstborn people and livestock across Egyptian society will die at midnight while Israel is distinguished, then leaves Pharaoh in anger; the chapter closes by restating Pharaoh’s refusal and Yahweh’s hardening.
whyItMatters: The final warning names a loss that reaches from royal house to servants and animals, making the cost of the confrontation unmistakable. The departure promised here leads directly to the Passover instructions and the night narrated in chapter 12.

context.author: Exodus names no writer of the finished book, though it depicts Moses writing particular words. Later tradition ascribes the Torah to him; its composition remains debated.
context.audience: Israel is addressed through its story of rescue, covenant, and worship; this chapter names no narrower first audience.
context.date: The book gives a relative story sequence but no secure external year for the events. The dating and formation of its finished text remain debated.
context.setting: Egypt during the last announced encounter with Pharaoh, with households across the land named in the impending judgment.
context.literaryForm: Short transitional warning containing preparations for departure, a speech on firstborn death, and a closing refusal notice.

before.text: Pharaoh has threatened Moses and rejected a departure that includes Israel’s livestock. The last announced plague now follows that failed negotiation.

here.text: The speech anticipates an expulsion, requested valuables from neighbors, and a midnight death among Egyptian firstborn.

after.text: The next chapter gives household instructions for the Passover night, then narrates the deaths, Pharaoh’s order to leave, and the departure.

outline.heading: One more plague and departure preparations
outline.note: Yahweh promises an expulsion and tells the people to ask Egyptian neighbors for precious items.

outline.heading: Firstborn death announced
outline.note: Moses warns of midnight deaths from Pharaoh’s household to the lowest household and livestock.

outline.heading: Israel distinguished; Moses departs angry
outline.note: The speech contrasts Israel’s safety and foresees Pharaoh’s servants urging departure.

outline.heading: Refusal and hardening restated
outline.note: The narrator closes by noting signs done, Pharaoh’s resistance, and divine hardening.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “I will bring yet one more plague on Pharaoh, and on Egypt; afterwards he will let you go. When he lets you go, he will surely thrust you out altogether.
keyVerses.why: The announced final plague is connected with Pharaoh driving Israel out completely.

keyVerses.text: and all the firstborn in the land of Egypt shall die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne, even to the firstborn of the female servant who is behind the mill, and all the firstborn of livestock.
keyVerses.why: The warning includes firstborn across social ranks and among livestock, not only Pharaoh’s son.

keyVerses.text: Moses and Aaron did all these wonders before Pharaoh, but Yahweh hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he didn’t let the children of Israel go out of his land.
keyVerses.why: The closing line restates the unresolved refusal and attributes hardening to Yahweh.

questions.question: How is the coming departure described before it happens?
questions.answer: Yahweh says Pharaoh will finally let Israel go and will drive them out altogether. The people are told to ask neighbors for silver and gold, and the narrator says they have favor with Egyptians.

questions.question: Who is included in the firstborn warning?
questions.answer: Moses names Pharaoh’s firstborn, the female servant’s firstborn, and firstborn livestock, covering high and low status. The later account broadens the examples again; this chapter gives no claim that every threatened household member made Pharaoh’s choices.

questions.question: What does “firstborn” mean in this warning?
questions.answer: It identifies the firstborn person in a household line and the first offspring of livestock named in the warning. Firstborn is a family position, not necessarily an infant; the speech’s force lies in how widely that position occurs across Egypt.

questions.question: Does Israel’s protection make the Egyptian deaths less severe?
questions.answer: No. The speech predicts a great cry throughout Egypt while saying even a dog will not bark against Israel. The contrast is part of the narrative’s claim about Yahweh’s distinction, not a reason to ignore the grief it forecasts.

questions.question: What does the image of a dog not moving its tongue convey?
questions.answer: It depicts complete quiet and safety around the children of Israel, humans and animals, at the time Egypt is expected to cry out. Moses uses it to mark a visible difference between the two groups.

questions.question: Who will ask Israel to leave?
questions.answer: Moses predicts Pharaoh’s servants will bow and urge him and the people following him to depart. The chapter presents this as part of the warning before the actual midnight events are narrated.

questions.question: How does this warning relate to Pharaoh’s hardened heart?
questions.answer: The ending says Yahweh hardened Pharaoh’s heart and that he did not release Israel despite the wonders. It reports the tension between divine action and royal refusal without explaining away the responsibility or harm involved.

questions.question: Has the final blow already happened by the end of chapter 11?
questions.answer: No. Moses announces what will occur about midnight and leaves in anger, while the narrator still describes Pharaoh refusing to release Israel. The Passover directions and the night itself come next.

glossary.def: The eldest offspring category named for royal, servant, and livestock households in the midnight warning.
Silver and gold items the Israelites are instructed to request from Egyptian neighbors before departure.
The final affliction announced against Pharaoh and Egypt before release is expected.
